content: 1. Iwashita et al. (2002) evaluated the use of the Fas2-ELISA and a modified rapid sedimentation technique for the diagnosis of Fasciola hepatica infection. Their findings were published in Revista de Medicina Herediana. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) convened an expert consultation in Vientiane, Lao PDR, in October 2009 to address foodborne trematode infections, taeniasis, and cysticercosis. The outcomes were published in 2011, including operational guidelines for eliminating human fascioliasis as a public health problem in the Americas. 3. Le et al. (2012) developed and validated a single-step duplex PCR assay for the simultaneous detection of Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica. This assay demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity and was published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology. 4. Calvani et al. (2017) introduced a molecular diagnostic workflow, termed Scrambled Eggs, for the sensitive detection of Fasciola species in fecal samples. Their study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 5. Cabada et al. (2017) compared recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with real-time PCR for detecting Fasciola hepatica in human stool samples. Their findings, published in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, highlighted the potential of RPA as a rapid diagnostic tool. 6. Carnevale et al. (2021) demonstrated the utility of PCR in a combined methodological approach to study human fascioliasis in endemic areas. Their research was published in Acta Parasitologica. 7. Alvarez Rojas et al. (2014) reviewed diagnostic techniques for Fasciola infections in animals, emphasizing the need for improved methods. This review was published in Advances in Parasitology. 8. Mezo et al. (2022) conducted a field evaluation of the enhanced MM3-COPRO ELISA test for diagnosing Fasciola hepatica infection in sheep. Their results were published in PLoS One. 9. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) emphasized the importance of a One Health approach to address health threats at the human-animal-environment interface during its 59th Directing Council meeting in 2021. 10. Mas-Coma et al. (2023) discussed the application of the One Health framework for controlling fascioliasis in human-endemic areas. Their work was published in Trends in Parasitology. 11. The WHO held an informal meeting in 2006 to evaluate the use of triclabendazole for fascioliasis control. The outcomes were published in 2007. 12. Favennec et al. (2003) conducted a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial to assess the efficacy of nitazoxanide in treating fascioliasis in adults and children in northern Peru. Their findings were published in Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 13. Cabada et al. (2016) reported treatment failures with triclabendazole in patients with fascioliasis in Cusco, Peru. This case series was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 14. Morales et al. (2021) documented triclabendazole treatment failures in preschool and school-aged children with Fasciola hepatica infection in Cusco, Peru. Their study was published in Emerging Infectious Diseases. 15. Gandhi et al. (2019) reviewed the use of triclabendazole for treating human fascioliasis, highlighting its efficacy and challenges. This review was published in Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 16. Terashima et al. (2021) conducted an observational study on the effectiveness and safety of multiple triclabendazole regimens in cases of treatment failure. Their findings were published in the Journal of Global Antimicrobial Resistance. 17. Marcos et al. (2021) discussed the threat of treatment failures with triclabendazole for human fascioliasis. Their review was published in Expert Review of Anti-Infective Therapy. 18. The WHO published a manual in 2006 on the coordinated use of anthelmintic drugs for controlling human helminth infections, targeting health professionals and program managers. 19. The WHO released a second edition of its guide for helminth control in school-aged children in 2011, providing strategies for program managers. 20. PAHO published operational guidelines in 2015 for integrated deworming activities to control soil-transmitted helminthiasis in Latin America and the Caribbean. 21. PAHO emphasized the importance of safety in administering medicines for neglected tropical diseases in its 2021 publication. 22. PAHO developed tools in 2017 for monitoring the coverage of integrated public health interventions, including vaccination and deworming for soil-transmitted helminthiasis. 23. Castro-Hermida et al. (2021) reviewed challenges in fasciolicide treatment for ruminant livestock. Their findings were published in Trends in Parasitology. 24. Rubilar et al. (1988) documented the use of triclabendazole for treating Fasciola hepatica infection in horses. Their study was published in Veterinary Record. 25. Gokbulut and McKellar (2018) reviewed anthelmintic drugs used in equine species, with a focus on their efficacy and safety. Their work was published in Veterinary Parasitology. 26. Matthews and Burden (2013) discussed common helminth infections in donkeys and their control in temperate regions. Their review was published in Equine Veterinary Education. 27. Fowler and Bravo (2010) edited the third edition of Medicine and Surgery of Camelids, providing comprehensive insights into camelid health. 28. Zerna et al. (2021) reviewed the current status of caprine fasciolosis control, emphasizing its overlooked impact. Their findings were published in Animals (Basel). 29. Alvarez et al. (2021) discussed the pharmacotherapeutics and drug resistance of flukicidal drugs in the second edition of Fasciolosis, edited by Dalton. 30. Love (2017) provided a comprehensive review of liver fluke infections in the third edition of Primefact 813, published by the New South Wales Department of Primary Industries. 31. Boray and Love (2017) discussed liver fluke disease in sheep and cattle in the fourth edition of Primefact 446, published by the New South Wales Department of Primary Industries. 32. Fairweather et al. (2020) reviewed drug resistance in liver flukes, highlighting its implications for treatment. Their work was published in the International Journal for Parasitology: Drugs and Drug Resistance. 33. The Control of Cattle Parasites Sustainably (COWS) initiative published a guide in 2017 on flukicide products for cattle. 34. Mas-Coma et al. (2020) investigated the role of sheep and cattle as reservoirs in hyperendemic areas of human fascioliasis in Bolivia, emphasizing a One Health approach. Their findings were published in Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 35. Mas-Coma et al. (2020) studied donkey fascioliasis within a One Health framework, focusing on its transmission capacity and epidemiology. Their research was published in Frontiers in Veterinary Science. 36. Mas-Coma et al. (2021) prioritized domestic pigs in One Health actions against fascioliasis in human-endemic areas, assessing their transmission capacity and reservoir role. Their findings were published in One Health. 37. Mas-Coma et al. (2021) documented fascioliasis in llamas in Andean endemic areas, analyzing their reservoir role and transmission capacity. Their study was published in Animals (Basel). 38. Howell and Williams (2020) reviewed the epidemiology and control of liver flukes in cattle and sheep. Their work was published in Veterinary Clinics of North America: Food Animal Practice. 39. John et al. (2019) reviewed parasite survival in silage and stored forages, focusing on Fasciola hepatica metacercariae. Their findings were published in Grass and Forage Science. 40. Mera y Sierra et al. (2020) investigated equines as reservoirs of human fascioliasis, focusing on their transmission capacity and pathogenicity. Their study was published in the Journal of Helminthology. 41. Mas-Coma et al. (2018) reviewed the diversity of infection sources, incidence factors, and prevention measures for human fascioliasis. Their work was published in Parasitology. 42. The WHO published a global strategy in 2021 to combat neglected tropical diseases through improved water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions. 43. PAHO released a practical guide in 2021 for collaboration between the WASH and health sectors to combat neglected tropical diseases. 44. Bargues et al. (2020) studied the genetic uniformity and geographical spread of lymnaeid vectors in Bolivia's hyperendemic areas, emphasizing a One Health approach. Their findings were published in Parasites & Vectors. 45. Bardales-Valdivia et al. (2021) assessed the spread of fascioliasis in Cajamarca, Peru, using seasonal follow-up of lymnaeid populations. Their study was published in One Health. 46. Rojas et al. (2010) discussed the challenges and opportunities for controlling fascioliasis in Cuba. Their work was published in Trends in Parasitology. 47. Sabourin et al. (2018) reviewed the impact of human activities on fascioliasis transmission. Their findings were published in Trends in Parasitology. 48. Alba et al. (2021) provided an integrative overview of the factors contributing to the emergence and re-emergence of fascioliasis. Their work was published in Parasitology. 49. Vázquez Perera and Sánchez Noda (2015) developed an illustrated guide for identifying freshwater gastropod mollusks in Cuba. Their work was published in Revista Cubana de Medicina Tropical. 50. Alda et al. (2018) developed a multiplex PCR assay to distinguish among three cryptic Galba species, intermediate hosts of Fasciola hepatica. Their findings were published in Veterinary Parasitology. 51. Caron et al. (2008) reviewed methods for detecting and quantifying digenetic infections in snail hosts, with a focus on Fasciola species. Their work was published in Parasitology Research. 52. Alba et al. (2016) assessed the FasciMol-ELISA for detecting Fasciola hepatica in field-collected Galba cubensis. Their study was published in Parasites & Vectors. 53. Cucher et al. (2006) utilized PCR to diagnose Fasciola hepatica in field-collected Lymnaea columella and Lymnaea viatrix snails. Their findings were published in Veterinary Parasitology. 54. Magalhães et al. (2004) detected Lymnaea columella infections by Fasciola hepatica using multiplex PCR. Their study was published in Memórias do Instituto Oswaldo Cruz. 55. Alba et al. (2015) developed a multiplex PCR for detecting Fasciola hepatica in the intermediate snail host Galba cubensis. Their findings were published in Veterinary Parasitology. 56. Mignagui et al. (2020) developed a duplex PCR for identifying Fasciola hepatica in lymnaeid snails. Their study was published in Revista de Investigación Agropecuaria. 57. The Ministry of Health of Peru published technical guidelines in 2020 for the surveillance, prevention, and control of human fascioliasis in Peru.
